sweep_summary: One stress-titled item for Tübatulabal: Jensen 1973 (Indiana U. PhD, 209 pp., committee incl. Voegelin). No open full text exists (HathiTrust not digitised, archive.org/Google Books/WorldCat/IUCAT/IUScholarWorks probes empty or blocked; Harvard HOLLIS/ProQuest restricted), but ProQuest serves a public 24-page preview (image-only; scanned here) that contains the two-page abstract, contents, introduction and ch. 1. The abstract states the stress rules outright: main stress on the right-most vowel of the word, secondary stress on even-numbered vowels leftward from it, glottal stops not counted as moras, length derived from stress. This confirms the catalog's fixed-final (QI, right-edge) main stress and right-to-left alternation from Voegelin 1935 §4, and refines the secondary-stress weight detail (Voegelin's moraic organic glottal stop is rejected). The stress chapter itself (ch. 5, pp. 144-162) remains unread: acquisition priority high (Harvard online access route already on the wishlist). Voegelin 1935 §4 pp. 75-79 was re-read from the on-disk Berkeley scan; the catalog's deciding quotation is verbatim-accurate and remains the deciding source.

new_statements.quote: The counting of glottal stops as moras is not permitted here, which also simplifies the stress process that consists of two rules; a main stress rule and an alternating or secondary stress rule. Main stress applies to the right-most vowel of a word and alternating stress applies to even-numbered vowels to the left of the main stress.

new_statements.reading: Final (right-most vowel) main stress, with secondary stress on every second vowel counting leftward from it — the same main-stress rule and right-to-left binary alternation the catalog codes from Voegelin 1935 §4 (main stress final; alternate stress every second mora backward). Jensen's counting unit differs in detail: long vowels are represented as two vowels (equivalent to Voegelin's two morae) but glottal stops are not moraic (Voegelin counts the organic glottal stop as one mora), and vowel length is treated as a consequence of stress rather than an independent alternating process. This confirms the catalog's edge=right / QI-fixed main stress and refines the secondary-stress weight statement (catalog 'heavy' field includes the organic glottal stop; Jensen rejects that). It is a reanalysis of Voegelin's data, read only from the abstract; Voegelin 1935 §4 pp. 75-79 (re-read in this sweep from the on-disk scan at, lines 1103-1240) remains the first-hand description and the catalog quote there is verbatim-accurate.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and every locator element (§4 p.75 main stress, p.76 alternation, fixed stress, no-mora-value closed syllables) are present verbatim in the held open Berkeley scan of Voegelin 1935 (PDF p.28-32 = printed 75-79). (2) The classification rests on the language's sole reference grammar, whose stress section is the primary source behind StressTyp2, Hayes 1981/1995 and Gordon 2002; the coding (final main stress, weight-blind primary; right-to-left every-second-mora secondary with CVV heavy, consonants moraless; enclitics outside the stress word) matches Voegelin's text and StressTyp2's U/1R + i(H,LL)R entries. (3) No better primary description exists: the language is dormant, no JIPA illustration or instrumental study surfaced in Crossref/Glottolog; the unheld items (Jensen 1973, Aion 2003) are theoretical reanalyses of the same data and are not openly available

sources.quote: The counting of glottal stops as moras is not permitted here, which also simplifies the stress process that consists of two rules; a main stress rule and an alternating or secondary stress rule. Main stress applies to the right-most vowel of a word and alternating stress applies to even-numbered vowels to the left of the main stress. [Abstract, pp. 1-2] ... It is found, contrary to the tradition that has developed about Tubatulabal, that there is no basis for the claim that there is an alternating length assignment rule. Rather, lengthening is a consequence of stress and can be predicted in the proper environment. [Abstract, p. 1]

sources.note: SPE-style reanalysis of Voegelin's (1935) data for verbs, affixes and particles (no new field description claimed; the abstract says the phonology 'was described in detail by C.F.Voegelin'). Two stress rules: main stress on the right-most (final) vowel of the word; alternating (secondary) stress on even-numbered vowels counting leftward from the main stress — i.e. the same final main stress and right-to-left binary alternation as Voegelin §4.
